own_scenes.desc: Hay un antes y un después de The Chronic (diciembre de 1992): samples de Parliament-Funkadelic, bajos lentos de Moog y músicos tocando encima, un sonido perezoso y amenazante a la vez, con Snoop Doggy Dogg, Nate Dogg, Daz, Warren G, Kurupt, The Lady of Rage y RBX. Lo publicó Death Row, fundada por Dr. Dre, The D.O.C., Dick Griffey y Marion «Suge» Knight, exguardaespaldas que «liberó» a Dre, D.O.C. y Michel’le de Ruthless con el dinero de un traficante preso, Michael «Harry-O» Harris; Interscope (Jimmy Iovine y Ted Field) lo financió y distribuyó. Snoop, de Long Beach, había hecho maquetas con Sir Jinx y formado 213 con Warren G y Nate Dogg; debutó en «Deep Cover». «Nuthin’ but a ‘G’ Thang» se grabó tres veces y vendió ocho millones (siete y medio a chavales blancos): con versiones de radio sin tacos, el gangsta llegó a todas partes, y SoundScan (1991), que contaba ventas reales, demostró su peso. Doggystyle (1993), con «Who Am I (What’s My Name)?» sobre «Atomic Dog», vendió ochocientos mil discos en una semana. Cold 187um (hijo y sobrino de los Hutch de Motown) reclama la invención del G-funk con Above the Law en Black Mafia Life; Warren G, fichado por Def Jam tras «Indo Smoke», lo llevó al pop con «Regulate» (sobre Michael McDonald). Death Row dominó con Dre, Snoop y Tupac y se hundió tras la muerte de este; Knight cumple veintiocho años de cárcel por atropellar mortalmente a Terry Carter en 2015.

refs.q: G-funk is heavily influenced by Parliament-Funkadelic, and that’s really all it comes down to.
refs.para: G-funk is heavily influenced by Parliament-Funkadelic, and that’s really all it comes down to. We always like to do things that just sounded out there and just kind of crazy. So that’s exactly what we were going for—the Moog, 808 drums, and then live musicianship on top of that.
refs.chapter: Cap. 16: A Higher Level of Execution

refs.para: Chris “The Glove” Taylor (DJ, producer): We’re DJs, right? We’re programmers, so all our shit got to be like a party. Like a house party starts off cool, it gets faster, and then it kind of eases out at the end, right? Put on The Chronic and play it all the way through at a party. You don’t even got to change it. It’s like a movie.
refs.chapter: Cap. 16: A Higher Level of Execution

refs.q: It’s just constantly about achieving a higher level of execution.
refs.para: Bun B (artist, UGK): It’s about not really trying to re-create the sound, but re-create the work ethic, right? Re-create the idea of how far-reaching music can be, and to not take any shortcuts when it came to the presentation of your music. Like if there’s a new technological advancement that’s being used in pop music, or rock music, or jazz music, or any kind of different art form, then we need to find a way that hip-hop can benefit from that kind of thing and incorporate it into what we’re doing. It’s just constantly about achieving a higher level of execution. That was definitely something that we still look at a person like Dr. Dre for inspiration for.
refs.chapter: Cap. 16: A Higher Level of Execution

refs.q: We broke with Black kids, but the other seven and a half million, that’s white kids.
refs.para: “ ‘G’ Thang” set a lot of trends, because it’s the first record to receive national airplay. I think we sold eight million records. We broke with Black kids, but the other seven and a half million, that’s white kids. So you can’t really just say that this is niche, urban, ghetto, whatever. That was kind of the first record, I think, that truly mainstreamed rap music and was history-setting in that respect.
